Follow-up of chronic problems.

CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Hypertension follow-up. 

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
The patient is a pleasant 72-year-old woman with hypertension, prior MI, mild hypercholesterolemia, and significant alcohol use disorder presenting for follow-up. At the last visit on 4/16 her BP was 130/90 after initially 150/100; she was prescribed hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) 12.5 mg PO daily and lisinopril 20 mg PO daily. SUBJECTIVE 
CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Full-spectrum STD testing.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Grace Ross is a new patient presenting for full-spectrum STD testing. She reports symptoms beginning last week of a “weird” vaginal discharge that smells different and has a different color and consistency than usual. She also notes soreness/pain on the right side of the vagina that has not gone away. She denies fevers or chills. She recently learned her boyfriend (partner of 3 years) has been having sexual encounters with other people, likely for about 3 months, and she wants to be evaluated for all STDs. She has a history of an abnormal Pap smear around age 20; her most recent Pap smear about 6 months ago was normal.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. STI exposure and screening (high risk) 
Assessment: New patient requesting comprehensive STD screening after learning partner has had multiple partners for several months. High-risk features include recent partner infidelity and a history of prior abnormal Pap smear (last Pap 6 months ago was normal). On pelvic exam today: no external lesions; normal labia; normal physiologic discharge (normal color and smell); cervix and vaginal wall normal; no cervical motion tenderness; no adnexal tenderness or masses. 
Plan: 
- Swabs obtained for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis. 
- Blood tests ordered for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis C. 
- Will call patient if any results are positive; patient may call in 3 days for results.

2. Vaginal discharge/odor and right-sided vaginal pain 
Assessment: One week of abnormal discharge with odor and right-sided vaginal soreness. Afebrile without chills. Pelvic exam reassuring with normal-appearing discharge and no cervical or adnexal tenderness. Differential includes cervicitis (GC/CT) and trichomoniasis; PID less likely given lack of cervical motion or adnexal tenderness and no systemic symptoms. 
Plan: 
- Diagnostic evaluation as above; no empiric treatment initiated today pending test results.

Follow-up instructions: 
- We will call with any abnormal/positive results; if no call, patient to call in 3 days for results. If all testing is normal, follow up at next annual checkup.

SUBJECTIVE 
CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Facial rash follow-up.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Jacqueline Miller presents for follow-up of a facial rash. She reports marked improvement when taking doxycycline twice daily for the first two weeks; after reducing to once daily last week based on pharmacist advice, the rash has plateaued and is not continuing to improve. She is not breastfeeding. Current regimen: sulfacetamide face wash twice daily (tolerated, not drying), metronidazole cream applied immediately after washing, and doxycycline (recently reduced to once daily). She did not start pimecrolimus (Elidel) due to concerns after reading about it and because it is cost-prohibitive with her insurance; she also checked prices for Eucrisa and found it more expensive. She is not using any moisturizer, Cetaphil cleanser, or Neutrogena wipes. She notes she feels sun-sensitive and is using sun precautions (hat). On clinician inspection today, there are a few faint erythematous papules on the bilateral medial cheeks and mild redness around/under the nostrils; not completely resolved.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Perioral dermatitis 
Assessment: Improved with doxycycline BID but plateaued after self-reduction to once daily; mild residual papules and perinasal erythema on exam. Not breastfeeding. Prefers to avoid topical steroids on face. 
Plan: 
- Increase doxycycline back to twice daily until rash is completely cleared, then continue once daily for one additional week before stopping. Counsel on potential GI upset/heartburn and strong photosensitivity; continue strict sun protection. 
- Start tacrolimus ointment (non-steroidal calcineurin inhibitor): apply a thin layer to involved facial rash areas twice daily until resolved. Counsel that brief tingling/flushing may occur for a few seconds after application and is not an allergy. Avoid topical steroids on the face due to risk of worsening and skin thinning. 
- Continue sulfacetamide face wash; may reduce to once daily if any dryness develops (use as tolerated). 
- Continue metronidazole cream after washing. 
- Add bland moisturizer as needed (e.g., Vanicream; small amounts of petroleum jelly if very dry). 
- Medication list/coverage: Cancel pimecrolimus (Elidel) due to cost; clindamycin removed from list. Prescription for tacrolimus to Metro Market pharmacy as discussed. Refills for doxycycline and metronidazole are adequate.

2. Rosacea (facial) 
Assessment: Overlapping rosacea component with persistent mild erythema/papules; photosensitivity noted. 
Plan: 
- Continue metronidazole cream and gentle skincare; avoid anti-aging or botanical products until reassessed. 
- Reinforce sun protection (hat already in use); avoid known triggers when possible.

3. Ocular rosacea 
Assessment: History/concern for ocular involvement; preventive eyelid hygiene recommended. 
Plan: 
- Gently wash eyelids once daily with a gentle cleanser (e.g., Vanicream). 
- Use a Bruder warm compress mask as needed.

Follow-up instructions: 
- Follow up in approximately 4 weeks. 
- If rash worsens or fails to improve, call or send MyChart message sooner. 
- For a mild flare after clearance, may try tacrolimus alone for a couple of days; if insufficient, restart doxycycline per above schedule. 
- Hold off on starting any new skincare products until next visit; discuss any planned additions first.

output.text:
SUBJECTIVE 
CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Nonhealing sore on right foot.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
The patient presents for evaluation of a right foot wound present for approximately 2–3 weeks. He reports no specific trauma. He recently bought a new pair of shoes for travel; due to his neuropathy he did not feel they were too tight, and the area began as a blister that has since worsened. He is no longer wearing those shoes. He was prescribed antibiotics by his PCP and finished the course yesterday, but the wound looks about the same. He denies pain (“can’t feel it”), fever, chills, or drainage, though he notes his sock sometimes sticks to the wound even when covered with a bandage. He has a history of stability issues at times. He has diabetes; his last hemoglobin A1c was “a little over 8.”

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Diabetic foot ulcer, right lateral/dorsal forefoot near 5th MTP, nonhealing 
Assessment: Nonhealing ulcer for 2–3 weeks following shoe-related pressure/friction in the setting of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Exam today notable for a ~1 x 2 inch circular wound with yellow slough and minimal granulation tissue; no surrounding erythema or cellulitis, no odor, no necrosis, no fluctuance, and no exposed bone. Afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Right foot x-ray shows no evidence of osteomyelitis. No current signs of soft tissue infection; completed an antibiotic course yesterday without improvement in appearance. Absent palpable DP/PT pulses with Doppler signals present raises concern for potential perfusion limitations impacting healing. 
Plan: 
- Wound debridement in clinic today to remove devitalized tissue. 
- Start collagenase ointment once daily; cover with a dry sterile dressing. Continue until wound is shrinking and healthy pink granulation tissue is present. 
- Offloading: Wear a surgical shoe to take pressure off the area; avoid the prior tight footwear. 
- No further antibiotics at this time given lack of clinical infection. 
- Order ankle-brachial index (ABI) to assess perfusion and healing potential. Refer to vascular specialist if ABI indicates suboptimal blood supply. 
- Return to clinic in 2 weeks for wound reassessment, sooner if increasing pain, redness, swelling, drainage, malodor, fever, or spreading erythema.

2. Diabetes mellitus with suboptimal control (A1c “a little over 8”) 
Assessment: Suboptimal glycemic control likely impairing wound healing. 
Plan: 
- Emphasize importance of improved glycemic control to facilitate wound healing. 
- Consider diabetes consult for additional dietary counseling and management strategies to reduce A1c.

Follow-up instructions: 
- Follow up in 2 weeks for wound check, or sooner for any signs of infection or worsening wound. 
- Proceed with ABI as ordered; potential vascular referral based on results. 
- Use surgical shoe consistently and apply collagenase with daily dressing changes as instructed.

SUBJECTIVE
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left knee pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient presents with left knee pain after twisting the knee while running with her 5-year-old niece about one week ago as the niece was learning to ride a bike without training wheels. She heard a “pop” at the time of injury. Since then she has been able to bear weight but has been limping, and the pain has been worsening. Pain is throbbing, located on both sides of the knee, worse medially. She reports swelling. She cannot take NSAIDs due to a recent ulcer and has been using acetaminophen, which provides only brief relief; she is aware not to take it too frequently. She applied kinesiology tape.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Left knee injury—suspected medial collateral ligament (MCL) strain
Assessment: Twisting mechanism with medial-predominant pain and tenderness, edema/effusion, limited range of motion with pain on flexion/extension. Stability testing negative (Lachman, varus/valgus), and left knee x-ray today shows no fracture or bony abnormality. Overall consistent with MCL strain rather than ligament tear.
Plan:
- Pain control: Start tramadol 50 mg twice daily. May use acetaminophen as needed for breakthrough pain; avoid exceeding recommended dosing.
- Immobilization: Knee immobilizer for 1 week to limit motion and reduce inflammation.
- Ice: Apply 3–4 times daily for 20–30 minutes each session.
- Activity: Avoid running for the next 3 weeks.
- Imaging/contingency: If symptoms worsen or fail to improve, contact the office; consider MRI to evaluate for internal derangement if clinical course is not improving.

2. History of recent ulcer—analgesic considerations
Assessment: Contraindication to NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen/Advil) due to recent ulcer.
Plan:
- Avoid NSAIDs.
- Use non-NSAID regimen as above (tramadol with PRN acetaminophen), with caution about acetaminophen overuse.

Follow-up instructions:
- Expect gradual improvement and return to normal activity in about 1 month if adhering to the plan.
- Update the office in a couple of days on progress, and call sooner for worsening pain, swelling, or new instability; MRI may be pursued if not improving.

["SUBJECTIVE 
CHIEF COMPLAINT 
Evaluation of kidney stone; follow-up for hypertension and type 2 diabetes; insomnia. 
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS 
Angela presents reporting a history of recurrent kidney stones, with approximately her 7th–8th episode. She went to the emergency room last week for flank pain but believes the stone passed about 3 days ago. She reports complete resolution of pain and no further hematuria. She received Percocet in the ER. She has seen a urologist in the past (about a year ago) and requests referral to Dr. Harris. She denies current chest pain or abdominal pain. 
Hypertension: On amlodipine (Norvasc) 2.5 mg, taken regularly. Clinic BP today was 150/90. She monitors at home 2–3 times per week with readings typically 130–140/60–70. She acknowledges difficulty reducing fast food intake due to time constraints; open to nutrition consult but hesitant about extra appointments. 
Diabetes mellitus type 2: On metformin 500 mg daily and taking as prescribed. She does not check blood glucose frequently but feels sugars have been “pretty good.” Last A1c after the prior visit was 6.7%. 
Insomnia: Intermittent difficulty falling asleep related to worry; meditation apps help. Sleep hygiene suboptimal (sleeps with TV on; phone by bedside). She has tried melatonin a couple of times without much benefit and prefers to avoid prescription sleep medications. 

"ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: 
1. Recurrent nephrolithiasis, currently asymptomatic (likely passed) 
Assessment: ER visit last week for suspected stone; patient reports stone passage ~3 days ago with resolution of pain and hematuria. Exam today without abdominal or CVA tenderness. Given frequent recurrences (7–8 lifetime), further evaluation warranted. 
Plan: 
- Obtain urinalysis and urine culture today to ensure resolution and screen for infection. 
- Refer to Urology (to Dr. Harris per patient preference) for evaluation of recurrent stones. 
- No analgesics needed currently; monitor for recurrence. 

2. Hypertension 
Assessment: Clinic BP 150/90 with home readings 130–140/60–70 on amlodipine 2.5 mg; likely white coat effect. BP improved from initial presentation (~180 systolic per chart review). 
Plan: 
- Continue amlodipine (Norvasc) 2.5 mg; no changes today. No refills needed now. 
- Continue home BP monitoring 2–3 times per week. 
- Nutrition consult placed to assist with dietary changes. 
- Counsel to limit sodium intake to ≤2300 mg/day and reduce fast food as able. 

3. Type 2 diabetes mellitus 
Assessment: On metformin 500 mg daily; last A1c 6.7%. Not routinely checking home glucose. 
Plan: 
- Continue metformin 500 mg daily. 
- Begin checking blood glucose before each meal to guide dietary choices and assess control. 

4. Insomnia 
Assessment: Intermittent, associated with worry; benefits from meditation apps; sleep hygiene suboptimal; prefers to avoid prescription hypnotics. 
Plan: 
- Recommend melatonin 10 mg as needed at bedtime. 
- Reinforce sleep hygiene: turn off electronics/TV at bedtime, dark/cool room; consider using phone’s sleep/do-not-disturb mode. 

5. Known systolic ejection murmur 
Assessment: Grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur noted again today, unchanged from prior. Asymptomatic. 
Plan: 
- Continue routine monitoring; no changes at this time. 

Follow-up instructions: 
- Return to clinic in 3 months for reassessment."]
